# On the Nature of Wandering Thoughts

I want to write about attention, because it seems to me that attention is the only currency we actually have, and we spend it carelessly, constantly, almost violently, on things that don't deserve it, while the things that do deserve it sit quietly at the edges of our days, waiting.

There's a particular quality to early morning light that I think about more than is probably reasonable. Not sunrise exactly, but the hour after—when the light has lost its dramatic redness and become something more workmanlike, more honest. It illuminates without performing. I've noticed that this is when I think most clearly, and I've wondered whether this is because of some circadian truth about cortisol and alertness, or whether it's simply because the world hasn't yet started demanding things of me. The phone hasn't buzzed. No one has asked me anything. There's a kind of mental nakedness available in those hours that disappears the moment the first notification arrives, and I think most of us have lost something significant in trading those quiet mornings for the immediate noise of connectivity.

I keep returning to this idea of noise versus signal, though I recognize it's become something of a cliché in discussions about modern life. Everyone complains about distraction now; it's almost become its own genre of complaint, a performance of concern about performance. But underneath the cliché there's something real, which is that human attention evolved for a world of immediate physical threats and rewards—the rustle in the grass, the ripening fruit—and it has been hijacked by systems explicitly designed to exploit those ancient circuits. We are, in some sense, fish that have been bred for thousands of years to recognize worms, suddenly confronted with an ocean full of shiny hooks. The worms were never the point. The hooks know this even if we don't.

But I don't want to write another jeremiad about phones and attention spans, because I think that conversation has calcified into something unproductive—a kind of moral preening where complaining about distraction has itself become a primary distraction. Instead I want to think about what attention actually is, phenomenologically, what it feels like from the inside.

When I pay attention to something—really attend to it—there's a kind of dissolution that happens. The boundary between me and the thing thins out. If I'm watching a bird forage in dead leaves, genuinely watching, not thinking about watching but actually watching, there's a moment where the watching and the bird and the leaves become a single field of awareness without much "me" left over to comment on it. This is, I think, what people are reaching for when they talk about meditation or flow states or mindfulness, though those words have become so saturated with self-help connotations that they've lost most of their descriptive power. What I'm describing isn't a technique. It's just what attention does when it's not being constantly redirected by anxiety or planning or the itch to check something.

The itch to check something—this seems important. There's a specific mental sensation, distinct from curiosity, distinct from desire, that precedes reaching for a phone. It's almost entirely empty of content. You don't check your phone because you want to know something specific; you check it because of a kind of psychic pressure that's built up, a sense that something might have happened, might be waiting, might require your attention. This feeling is almost completely disconnected from whether anything has, in fact, happened. The feeling exists prior to and independent of any actual information. I find this fascinating and slightly horrifying—that we've built machines that generate anticipatory anxiety as a renewable resource, that mine us for this specific psychological ore.

I think about this in relation to boredom, too, because boredom has nearly disappeared from contemporary life, and I'm not sure this is the unambiguous good it's often portrayed as. Boredom used to be a kind of pressure that built up until it forced creative or reflective action—you'd be bored enough that you'd start drawing on a napkin, or staring out a window until your mind wandered somewhere unexpected, or you'd finally pick up that book you'd been meaning to read. Boredom was uncomfortable but generative. It was the gap in which thought could happen. Now the gap gets filled automatically, instantly, by infinite scroll, and I wonder what we've lost in the elimination of that particular discomfort. Maybe nothing. Maybe boredom was never actually productive and we're just nostalgic for a state we didn't enjoy at the time, the way people romanticize hardship retrospectively while having hated it in the moment. But I suspect something real has been lost, some fertile discomfort that used to push the mind toward unexpected territories.

I want to write about silence, too, though silence is hard to write about because the act of writing about it requires breaking it.

I live near enough to nature that I can walk into something resembling wilderness within twenty minutes, and I've started doing this more often, specifically to encounter silence, or what passes for silence in a world with distant highways and occasional aircraft. What I notice is that silence is never actually silent. There's always something—wind moving through different textures of vegetation, which all have their own distinct sound; insects; the small sounds of my own body, breathing, blood moving, the creak of joints. True silence, the absence of all sound, would probably be a kind of psychological violence; I think sensory deprivation experiments have shown this, that total silence eventually becomes its own form of torment, the brain manufacturing phantom sounds to fill the void, hallucinating texture into emptiness because the alternative is unbearable. So when I say I seek silence, what I actually mean is I seek a particular density of sound, a specific texture of acoustic information that feels different from the density of human-generated noise—voices, engines, notifications, music. There's something about non-human sound that allows a different quality of thought, though I can't fully articulate why. Maybe it's because non-human sound doesn't address us. A voice, even a stranger's voice on the street, contains an implicit demand for interpretation—are they talking to me, about me, near me, does this concern me. Wind doesn't do this. Wind is sound without address, without claim on us, and maybe that's why it allows the mind to settle into itself rather than remaining in a state of perpetual low-grade readiness to respond.

This makes me think about readiness as a state, because I think most of contemporary life is conducted in a state of low-grade readiness that we've simply normalized to the point of not noticing it. We are always slightly braced. The body holds tension it isn't aware of holding. I notice this most clearly in retrospect, after I've spent time somewhere that doesn't require readiness—after a few days away from connectivity, when I return and feel the click of re-entering vigilance, like a held breath I didn't know I was holding being released and then, almost immediately, held again. There's a specific muscular signature to modern attention, I think, a kind of perpetual mobilization for response, and I wonder what it would mean to live without that, whether it's even possible anymore, or whether we've simply built a world that requires this readiness as the price of participation.

I don't think the answer is to reject technology wholesale, which seems both impractical and slightly self-righteous, a kind of performance of virtue through deprivation that usually doesn't survive contact with actual need. I use these tools. I depend on them. I'm not interested in pretending otherwise or in some fantasy of return to a pre-digital purity that probably never existed in the form we imagine it. What I'm interested in is something more granular: the question of what specific practices, what specific habits of attention, allow for both connectivity and depth, for both the practical use of these tools and the preservation of whatever it is that gets eroded by their overuse.

I keep thinking about an idea I encountered once, possibly apocryphal, possibly distorted by my memory into something more useful than its original form, about how certain traditional societies didn't have a word for "bored" because they didn't conceive of unoccupied time as a problem requiring solution. Idleness wasn't a gap to be filled; it was simply a state, neutral, sometimes even valuable. I don't know if this is historically accurate—a lot of claims about traditional societies turn out to be projections, romanticizations, the noble savage trope wearing new clothes—but the idea itself is useful regardless of its historical accuracy, because it points toward something: the conception of unoccupied attention as a problem is itself a culturally specific development, not a universal human condition. We've been trained, recently and thoroughly, to experience our own unoccupied minds as a kind of emergency.

This training has happened so fast, in evolutionary terms, that I don't think we should be surprised we're bad at resisting it, or even that resistance is quite the right framework. It's only been twenty years or so since smartphones, less than that since they became truly ubiquitous, and the systems designed to capture attention have had enormous resources and enormous incentive to become extremely good at their jobs. We're not failing some test of willpower; we're encountering, for the first time in human history, technologies explicitly optimized against our own stated interests, technologies whose success is measured by their ability to capture something we would, if asked directly, say we didn't want captured. This is a strange position to be in. It's a bit like being hunted by something that knows exactly what you find delicious and is made entirely of that thing, dressed up to look unrelated to the hunt at all.

I wonder sometimes whether future generations will look back on this period—our period, now, this specific decade—the way we look back on early industrial cities choking on coal smoke, recognizing a kind of obvious environmental hazard that the people living within it couldn't quite see because they were too immersed in it, too dependent on the systems producing it, too lacking in the comparative vantage point that only comes later, after enough damage has accumulated that the pattern becomes undeniable. Maybe attention pollution will eventually get the same treatment as air pollution—recognized, regulated, mitigated, even if imperfectly. Or maybe we'll simply adapt, the way people adapted to factory whistles and clock time, find new equilibria that look nothing like the boredom-tolerant, silence-comfortable humans of the deeper past, and that adaptation won't be experienced as loss because the comparison point will have vanished from living memory.

I don't know which of these futures is more likely, or whether there's some entirely different future neither resembles. What I know is that right now, today, in this specific moment of historical transition, there's something valuable in noticing the texture of my own attention—where it goes, what it's pulled toward, what it resists, what specific qualities of experience seem to deepen it versus fragment it.

I notice, for instance, that attention deepens with specificity. If I'm walking and simply registering "trees, sky, path," my mind stays shallow, skating along the surface of categories. But if I notice this specific oak, the way its bark splits into something like canyons in miniature, the way one branch has clearly been struck by lightning at some point and grown around the wound in a thick scarred whorl—the specificity itself seems to pull me down into a different relationship with the world. Generality keeps us at the surface. Specificity is a kind of depth charge. This might explain something about why certain kinds of writing feel alive and others feel dead on the page—the live ones are tracking specific, granular, embodied detail, while the dead ones are gesturing at categories, at the idea of a tree rather than this tree, at the idea of grief rather than this particular grief with its particular weight and texture and smell.

I think this is why poetry, at its best, functions almost like a technology for attention—not metaphorically but literally, a tool whose function is to force specificity, to prevent the mind from sliding into the comfortable generality that requires no real engagement. A good poem won't let you skim. It forces you to actually look at the thing being described, because the language itself resists the kind of pattern-matching shortcut that lets us process most of our daily experience without really experiencing it at all.

I wonder if this is also why certain kinds of grief or pain demand so much attention—because they refuse generality, they insist on their specificity, they won't let you process them as "a sad thing" but force you into this particular absence, this particular silence where a voice used to be, this particular Tuesday that will now always be different from every other Tuesday. Maybe pain is one of the few remaining forces strong enough to compete with our manufactured distractions, the rare thing that can out-shout the phone, that refuses to be scrolled past. This isn't a cheerful thought, but it might be a true one, or true enough to be worth sitting with.

I've been writing for a while now without quite knowing where this is going, which seems appropriate to the subject matter—an essay about attention that wanders, that follows its own associative logic rather than marching toward a predetermined conclusion. Maybe that's the point, or as close to a point as I'm going to get: that thought, left to its own devices, doesn't move in straight lines. It moves in this kind of associative drift, one thing calling up another, attention following its own strange logic that only looks like logic in retrospect, after you've drawn the lines connecting the dots.

I don't think there's a neat lesson here, no five-step program for reclaiming your attention, no triumphant resolution where I report having solved this problem in my own life. I haven't solved it. I check my phone too often. I lose hours to feeds that give nothing back. But I notice it more now, this push and pull between depth and fragmentation, and noticing seems like a precondition for anything else, even if it's not sufficient on its own. Maybe that's the most honest place to end—not with a solution but with an ongoing attention to attention itself, a willingness to keep noticing the noticing, to ask, again and again, what's pulling at me right now, and whether it deserves what it's asking for.
